patient_summary:
You're feeling chest pain, and it's been getting worse. You have a history of diabetes, heart problems, and had a heart procedure before. You've been taking some medicine for your heart and diabetes. You also take a special medicine called aspirin to help your heart. You also use a medicine called insulin to help control your diabetes. You've been using nitroglycerin tablets when you feel pain, and they've helped a little bit.

You've also been feeling short of breath, have some nausea, and have had some vomiting. You've taken some nitroglycerin, and now your pain is a 4 out of 10. You've had this pain for about an hour. You're a little worried because you've had similar pain before, and it's gotten worse when you walk.

You haven't had any fever or chills, and you haven't had any bleeding. You've been eating normally and have been drinking water. You've been smoking a lot of cigarettes, but you're trying to quit.

You've been feeling a little better with the nitroglycerin, but you should still see your doctor if your pain gets worse or doesn't go away. If you feel short of breath or have trouble breathing, you should go to the hospital right away. If you have any other symptoms like fever or chills, you should also go to the hospital. You should also tell your doctor if you have any allergic reactions, like an allergic reaction to penicillin. You should also mention that you take 50 units of insulin in the morning and 50 mg of nitroglycerin as needed for chest pain.
caregiver_checklist: Give the patient 3 nitroglycerin tablets sublingually and monitor for any relief.
Check the patient’s blood pressure and heart rate regularly.
Watch for signs of worsening pain, shortness of breath, or new symptoms like fever or chills.
Call 911 if the patient’s pain increases to a 9 or higher, or if they experience shortness of breath, chest tightness, or dizziness.
Schedule a follow-up appointment with the cardiologist in 2 weeks.
Call the healthcare provider if the patient’s symptoms persist or worsen.
Watch for signs of dehydration, such as dry mouth, decreased urination, or dizziness upon standing.
Call the healthcare provider if the patient experiences any bleeding episodes.
Schedule a blood glucose test to monitor for diabetes complications.
Call the healthcare provider if the patient has any new or worsening symptoms.
Take the patient’s aspirin as prescribed (81 milligrams QDay).
Administer the patient’s insulin (50 units, 50 mg) as needed (PRN) for blood sugar management.
Call the healthcare provider if the patient experiences any allergic reactions to medications, including penicillin.
child_explanation: You had a little ache in your chest, like a whisper at first. But it grew louder, like a loud noise. You told the grown-ups about it, and they're taking good care of you. They know how to help. You're not sick, just having a small problem. The doctors are checking to make sure you're okay. They're like a team of tiny helpers, watching over you. You're doing well, and they're helping you feel better.
source_text: CHIEF COMPLAINT: , Chest pain.,HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:,  The patient is a 40-year-old white male who presents with a chief complaint of "chest pain".,The patient is diabetic and has a prior history of coronary artery disease.  The patient presents today stating that his chest pain started yesterday evening and has been somewhat intermittent.  The severity of the pain has progressively increased.  He describes the pain as a sharp and heavy pain which radiates to his neck & left arm.  He ranks the pain a 7 on a scale of 1-10.  He admits some shortness of breath & diaphoresis.  He states that he has had nausea & 3 episodes of vomiting tonight.  He denies any fever or chills.  He admits prior episodes of similar pain prior to his PTCA in 1995.  He states the pain is somewhat worse with walking and seems to be relieved with rest.  There is no change in pain with positioning.  He states that he took 3 nitroglycerin tablets sublingually over the past 1 hour, which he states has partially relieved his pain.  The patient ranks his present pain a 4 on a scale of 1-10.  The most recent episode of pain has lasted one-hour.,The patient denies any history of recent surgery, head trauma, recent stroke, abnormal bleeding such as blood in urine or stool or nosebleed.,REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:,  All other systems reviewed & are negative.,PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:,  Diabetes mellitus type II, hypertension, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, status post PTCA in 1995 by Dr. ABC.,SOCIAL HISTORY: , Denies alcohol or drugs.  Smokes 2 packs of cigarettes per day.  Works as a banker.,FAMILY HISTORY: , Positive for coronary artery disease (father & brother).,MEDICATIONS: , Aspirin 81 milligrams QDay.  Humulin N. insulin 50 units in a.m.  HCTZ 50 mg QDay.  Nitroglycerin 1/150 sublingually PRN chest pain.,ALLERGIES: , Penicillin.,PHYSICAL EXAM: , The patient is a 40-year-old white male.,General:  The patient is moderately obese but he is otherwise well developed & well nourished.  He appears in moderate discomfort but there is no evidence of distress.  He is alert, and oriented to person place and circumstance.  There is no evidence of respiratory distress.  The patient ambulates
